$comment: The one rule two shortest-round-tripping serialisers still disagree about. `input` is a JSON number literal, parsed by each language's own parser into an IEEE-754 double; `expected` is what RFC 8785 §3.2.2.3 requires, which is ECMAScript's Number::toString, read off a real ECMAScript engine. Python's repr is also shortest-round-tripping and is NOT this function: it disagrees about where exponential notation begins at both ends, and about whether a whole float keeps its `.0`. Every case below is one a naive implementation gets wrong.

cases.name: the round-trip efficiency the reference battery is published at
a trailing zero is not part of the number
a whole number carries no decimal point
cases.source_spelling: 100.0 — Python's repr is `100.0` and would hash differently

cases.name: an integer
zero
negative zero is zero
cases.source_spelling: -0.0 — a signed zero is a distinction JSON cannot carry and a hash must not invent

cases.name: a negative
one half
a tenth, which is not exactly representable
the last exponent that stays decimal, going small
the first exponent that goes exponential, going small
cases.source_spelling: 1e-7 — Python's repr is `1e-07`, with a zero-padded exponent

cases.name: the last exponent that stays decimal, going large
the first exponent that goes exponential, going large
seventeen significant digits, still decimal
an integer beyond exact double precision
cases.source_spelling: 9007199254740993 — 2^53 + 1, which no double holds; both sides must round it the same way before serialising, or a Python bignum and a JavaScript double disagree

cases.name: a value with a fractional part and a large integer part
the smallest positive double
the largest finite double
the published initial state of charge
the default minimum state of charge
the default maximum state of charge
